chapter: Political Science: Gender, Religion and Caste
name: Gender and Politics: Public and Private Division

scenes.animation: A Diwali evening at home. Zippy's cartoon uncle lounges with the TV remote while the aunt cooks, cleans and hangs lights all at once with six arms. Zippy points: 'Isn't that just natural?'

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Housework is just naturally a woman's job, right?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Not natural at all. It's based on social expectations and stereotypes. Let's look at gender division.

scenes.animation: A house splits in two: the inside labelled 'Private: housework, bringing up children' in soft colours, the outside labelled 'Public: paid work, politics'. A dotted line divides them. Then the chef, tailor and dhobi outside are shown as men doing the same tasks for pay.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Gender division is a form of hierarchical social division seen everywhere. It is based on the sexual division of labour.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Women do all work inside the home, such as cooking, cleaning, washing clothes and looking after children. Men do all work outside the home.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yet when these jobs are paid for, men are ready to do them. Most tailors or cooks in hotels are men. So the division isn't about biology.

scenes.animation: A stopwatch labelled 'Average working day' shows a woman's bar extending one hour beyond a man's. The woman's bar is coloured grey with a label 'Much of it unpaid and unrecognised'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: On an average, an Indian woman works one hour more than an average man every day. Much of her work is not paid, and therefore often not valued.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: An extra hour every day? That's not fair.

scenes.animation: Crowds march with placards 'Equal voting rights', 'Equal education', 'Equal work'. A label 'Feminist movements' appears. A world map lights up Sweden, Norway and Finland with a bright glow: 'High women's participation in public life'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Women in different parts of the world organised and agitated for equal rights, including voting rights. They also demanded enhancing the political and legal status of women and improving their educational and career opportunities.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Radical women's movements aimed at equality in personal and family life as well. These are called feminist movements.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Today, in Scandinavian countries such as Sweden, Norway and Finland, the participation of women in public life is very high.

scenes.animation: An exam question card: 'What is sexual division of labour?' A 'Board Tip' sticker highlights the key phrase 'all work inside the home is done by women'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: define sexual division of labour clearly, and say that it is a social belief, not a biological fact.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a house-and-world icon. Points appear: '1. Gender division is social, not natural', '2. Women work one hour more daily, often unpaid', '3. Feminist movements for equality'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: gender division is based on social expectations, not biology.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: Indian women work about one hour more each day than men, much of it unpaid.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: feminist movements demanded equality in public, personal and family life.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Uncle, the remote is now a shared resource. Help with the lights!

chapter: Political Science: Gender, Religion and Caste
name: Women's Disadvantages and Political Representation

scenes.animation: A school report card on a noticeboard shows girls topping the class. Zippy cheers, then sees a second board labelled 'Higher studies' with fewer girls' names. His smile drops.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Girls top the boards, so everything's equal now, right?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Girls often perform better, yet they drop out more, because parents prefer to spend on boys' education. India is still a male dominated, patriarchal society.

scenes.animation: Four cards flip open: 'Literacy: lower among women', 'Fewer women in highly paid jobs', 'Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, but unequal wages in practice', 'Child sex ratio: 919 girls per 1000 boys'. The last card flashes red.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The literacy rate among women is still lower than among men. The proportion of women among the highly paid and valued jobs is still very small.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 provides that equal wages should be paid to equal work. However, in almost all areas of work, women are paid less than men.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In many parts of India, parents prefer sons. This has led to a decline in the child sex ratio, the number of girl children per thousand boys, to merely 919. Women also face harassment, exploitation and violence.

scenes.animation: A bar chart rises: 'Women in Lok Sabha: 14.36% in 2019, first time crossing 14%' and 'State assemblies: less than 5%'. A tall dotted target line marked 'One-third' hovers far above both bars. Then a village panchayat hall fills with women members.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In India, the proportion of women in the legislature has been very low. The percentage of elected women members in the Lok Sabha touched 14.36 per cent of its total strength for the first time in 2019. Their share in state assemblies is less than 5 per cent.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One way to solve this is to have a fair proportion of women among elected representatives. In panchayats and municipalities, one-third of seats are reserved for women. Now there are more than 10 lakh elected women representatives in rural and urban local bodies.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Women's organisations have demanded a similar reservation of at least one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies.

scenes.animation: A 'Fun Fact' badge pops up beside a Parliament building with a new law scroll: '2023: Law passed to reserve one-third seats for women'. A 'Board Tip' sticker follows.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Did that demand ever go anywhere?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Fun fact: in 2023, Parliament passed a law to reserve one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies for women. It will come into effect in the future.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: for your exam, stick to the textbook points: low representation in legislatures and one-third reservation in local bodies.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a ballot box icon wearing a bindi. Points appear: '1. Lower literacy, wages, child sex ratio 919', '2. Lok Sabha 14.36% (2019); assemblies under 5%', '3. One-third reservation in local bodies'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: women face disadvantages in literacy, jobs, wages and the child sex ratio.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: women were only 14.36 per cent of the Lok Sabha in 2019, and less than 5 per cent in state assemblies.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: one-third reservation in local bodies has brought many women into politics.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Girls topping boards and topping ballots. That's the goal.

chapter: Political Science: Gender, Religion and Caste
name: Religion, Communalism and Politics

scenes.animation: A colourful street shows a temple, a mosque, a gurdwara and a church side by side, with neighbours sharing sweets. Then a shadowy figure with a megaphone labelled 'Communal politics' tries to draw walls between the buildings.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Everyone was sharing sweets. Who's building walls now?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's communal politics. Religion itself isn't the problem. The problem begins when religion is seen as the basis of the nation.

scenes.animation: Three green tick cards appear: 'Gandhiji: politics guided by ethics from religion', 'Human rights groups: protect minorities', 'Women's movement: family laws discriminate against women'. A caption: 'Religion and politics can interact positively'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Gandhiji used to say that religion can never be separated from politics. By religion he meant moral values that inform all religions.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Human rights groups have argued that most victims of communal riots are from religious minorities. The women's movement has argued that family laws of all religions discriminate against women.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Every citizen should be able to express needs and interests as a member of a religious community, and political power should be able to regulate religion to prevent discrimination.

scenes.animation: A staircase of four steps builds, each darker than the last: 'Everyday beliefs and stereotypes', 'Political dominance of one's own community', 'Political mobilisation on religious lines', 'Communal violence, riots and massacre'. A small 1947 Partition image appears at the bottom step.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Communalism can take various forms. It can be expressed in everyday beliefs, like religious prejudices and stereotypes, and belief in the superiority of one's religion.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A communal mind often seeks political dominance of its own religious community. Political mobilisation on religious lines is another frequent form, using sacred symbols, religious leaders and emotional appeal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Sometimes communalism takes its most ugly form of communal violence, riots and massacre. India and Pakistan suffered some of the worst communal riots at the time of Partition.

scenes.animation: The Constitution opens, and four glowing pillars rise under the word 'Secular State': 'No official religion', 'Freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion', 'No discrimination on grounds of religion', 'State can intervene to ensure equality, e.g. ban on untouchability'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Communalism was one of the major challenges to democracy, so the makers of our Constitution chose the model of a secular state.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: There is no official religion for the Indian state. The Constitution provides freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion, or not to follow any. It prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: At the same time, the Constitution allows the state to intervene in matters of religion to ensure equality within religious communities. For example, it bans untouchability.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: the forms of communalism and the features of a secular state are both frequent questions.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the four places of worship icon. Points appear: '1. Religion in politics is not always bad', '2. Communalism: beliefs, dominance, mobilisation, violence', '3. India: a secular state'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: religion and politics can interact without harm.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: communalism ranges from everyday stereotypes to violence.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: our Constitution makes India a secular state with no official religion.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Walls down. Pass the sweets.

chapter: Political Science: Gender, Religion and Caste
name: Caste and Politics

scenes.animation: Zippy sits at a lunch table where cartoon kids are sorted by badges. He rips off the badges and mixes the seating. Neo nods, and a gallery of portraits appears: 'Jotiba Phule', 'Gandhiji', 'B.R. Ambedkar', 'Periyar Ramaswami Naicker'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why should birth decide where you sit or what you do?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It shouldn't. Political leaders and social reformers like Jotiba Phule, Gandhiji, B.R. Ambedkar and Periyar Ramaswami Naicker worked to establish a society without caste inequalities.

scenes.animation: An arrow labelled 'Change' sweeps through a city: school buildings, factories and crowded buses mix people freely. Labels pop up: 'Urbanisation', 'Literacy and education', 'Occupational mobility', 'Constitution prohibits caste discrimination'. A shadow still lingers labelled 'Untouchability not fully ended'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Caste divisions are special to India. In the caste system, hereditary occupational division was sanctioned by rituals.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Partly due to their efforts and partly due to socio-economic changes like urbanisation, growth of literacy, occupational mobility and weakening of landlords in villages, caste hierarchy is breaking down.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Our Constitution prohibited any caste-based discrimination. Yet untouchability has not ended completely, and caste continues to be closely linked to economic status.

scenes.animation: A party office: leaders study a constituency chart with coloured caste slices before choosing a candidate. A ballot box then appears with 'Universal adult franchise: one person, one vote', and people from all castes queue together. A pie chart shows no slice above half: 'No constituency has a clear majority of one caste'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Caste in politics takes several forms. When parties choose candidates, they keep in mind the caste composition of the electorate. Parties and candidates make appeals to caste sentiment.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Universal adult franchise and one-person-one-vote have compelled leaders to gain political support. They also brought new consciousness among people of castes that were treated as inferior.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So elections are all about caste?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No. No parliamentary constituency in the country has a clear majority of one single caste. Voters have strong attachment to parties, and the ruling party and sitting MP often lose elections. Caste alone cannot determine results.

scenes.animation: Reverse arrow: 'Politics in caste'. Small caste groups merge into a bigger circle, circles form alliances, and two big new labels appear: 'Backward' and 'Forward'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It is not politics that gets caste-ridden, it is caste that gets politicised. Each caste group tries to become bigger by incorporating neighbouring castes, enters into coalitions with others, and new kinds of caste groups like backward and forward emerge.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: expressing caste identity in politics allowed disadvantaged groups to demand their share of power. But focusing only on caste can divert attention from issues like poverty and development.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a mixed lunch table icon. Points appear: '1. Reformers and social change weakened caste hierarchy', '2. Caste in politics: candidates, appeals, franchise', '3. Politics in caste: groups merge and ally'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: reformers and socio-economic change weakened the caste hierarchy, but inequalities remain.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: caste shapes candidate choice and appeals, but cannot alone decide elections.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: politics also changes caste, creating bigger groups and alliances.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: New seating plan: sit wherever you like.
